key_insight: This paper reframes watermarking as an information-theoretic forensic problem: different watermark goals—detecting machine text, identifying the producer, recovering a payload, or localizing surviving content—can all be analyzed by how much secret information is revealed per token. The key result is a unified way to understand the sample length needed for each forensic task.
problem_solved: It addresses the lack of a common theory for evaluating generative-model watermarks beyond simple machine-vs-human detection. The paper asks how many generated tokens are needed to reliably recover different kinds of watermark evidence, including user attribution, hidden messages, and edit-robust localization.
method: Define a secret S carried by the watermark, such as user identity or payload.
Introduce an information profile ν(t)=I(S;X_t | X_<t) to quantify how much each generated token reveals about the secret.
Use this profile to derive sample-length costs for a forensic ladder of tasks, from detection to attribution and localization.
impact: For ML practitioners, this provides a principled framework for designing and benchmarking watermark schemes instead of relying only on empirical detection accuracy. It can guide choices about watermark strength, robustness, and the trade-off between utility and forensic recoverability.
visual_elements: A forensic ladder diagram showing detection, attribution, payload recovery, and localization as increasing levels of watermark analysis.
A token-by-token information flow chart illustrating ν(t)=I(S;X_t | X_<t).
A comparison table mapping each forensic task to its required sample length n.
An icon set for secret, generated text, attacker/editing, and recovered watermark evidence.
paper_title: Watermark Forensics for Generative Models: An Information-Theoretic Perspective
paper_authors: Xiaoyu Li, Zheng Gao, Xiaoyan Feng, Jiaojiao Jiang, Yulei Sui
